title: Fit a servo horn onto its splined output shaft with its arm on the zero mark
instruction: Fit the white servo horn onto the servo's splined output shaft with its arm lined up on the engraved zero mark, then let go.
context: Building or repairing a robot arm means fitting a horn onto the 25-tooth output shaft of each joint's servo. The horn seats at only 25 angles, 14.4 degrees apart, so its arm is lined up on the zero mark before it is pressed on; pressed where it happens to land, the joint is off by whole teeth and every later calibration inherits the error. The horn is a small part: it has to be set squarely on the shaft, turned onto the mark while it still rests on the tooth crests, and pressed home with about 32 N. This is a step in assembling the arms that robot data are collected with; a robot that can do it can help build and repair robots.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases (x away from the arms, y to the left); heights over the bench top. One fixed layout, nothing varies by seed. A TowerPro MG996R servo (black, 40.7 x 19.7 x 42.9 mm over all with its shaft, 55 g), fixed: hanging by its mounting ears on two aluminium posts screwed to the bench, long axis along x, its middle at x 43, y -22; its brass output shaft (5.9 mm across, 25 teeth) points up at the end of the case nearer the arms, its top 42.9 mm over the bench. A white zero mark 24 x 1.2 mm is engraved on the case top from the shaft's boss outwards, away from the arms. The single-arm horn from the servo's own horn set (white nylon, hub 14 mm across and 7 mm tall, arm 28 mm long, 7 mm wide and 2 mm thick, 4 g) lies on the bench at x 38, y -33, its arm 68 degrees from the mark's direction (4 degrees off a tooth position). Nothing else is on the bench. Both arms start in their ready pose; servo and horn lie before the right arm.
scoring: Only the state at the end of the trial counts; a horn seated on another tooth, pulled off and refitted on the mark's tooth scores as it ends. On the shaft: the hub's axis within 0.6 mm of the shaft's and upright within 8 degrees. Engaged: the horn has gone 0.2 mm or more down with its teeth in the shaft's and no longer turns. 0: engaged with the arm more than 2.0 degrees from the mark (another tooth), or not on the shaft, or nothing below. 0.25: on the shaft, resting on the tooth crests, the arm within 3.0 degrees of the mark. 0.5: engaged on the mark's tooth (arm within 2.0 degrees), 0.5 mm or more down. 0.75: the same, 3.0 mm or more down (0.5 mm or less proud). 1.0: also the horn at rest and both grippers 3 cm or more from it; held for 1 s the trial ends as a success. Real bench: a photo from above with a ruler laid along the mark for the arm's angle; whether the arm turns when pushed gently; a caliper's depth rod for the gap between hub and boss (3.0 mm or less) and a 0.5 mm feeler under the hub for the last two levels; the video for the release.
reset_notes: Pull the horn off (about 10 N), look at its teeth and replace a horn whose teeth are worn or crushed; lay it on its mark on the bench with its arm 68 degrees from the servo's mark. The servo is not powered; its shaft is left where the zero mark was set.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; no splines. The shaft's top is a sprung stop: off a tooth position the horn stands 3.5 mm proud; within 2.0 degrees it goes down under 32 N and locks. The 3.5 mm and 32 N are quoted from the earlier submission, not measured by us; the 2.0 degrees and 10 N pull-off are assumed. On the crests the horn is held by joints with 200 g of inertia (4 g when free). It must be set on the shaft within about 0.1 mm; real chamfers are more forgiving. Details: README.
